extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, IPR petitioners/defendants, PTAB counsel and examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and guidance for Director-level review of PTAB institution decisions in inter partes review, focused on assessing obviousness (motivation to combine, expectation of success), treatment of expert testimony and secondary considerations (including simultaneous invention), and when discretionary denial under 35 U.S.C. § 314(a) is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansive and flexible approach to obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessing obviousness is based on an 'expansive and flexible approach' that 'need not seek out precise teachings directed to the specific subject matter of the challenged claim, for a court can take account of the inferences and creative steps that a person of ordinary skill in the art would employ.' (KSR; Updated Guidance; MPEP §2141).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider market forces, design incentives, interrelated teachings of multiple patents, any need or problem known in the field at the time of invention, and the background knowledge, creativity, and common sense of a person of ordinary skill. Do not apply rigid rules that preclude common-sense inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine (institution stage)
rubrics_metrics.description: The motivation-to-combine inquiry asks whether a skilled artisan 'not only could have made but would have been motivated to make the combinations . . . of prior art to arrive at the claimed invention.' (Auris Health v. Intuitive Surgical; Belden).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At institution, the petitioner must demonstrate a sufficient motivation to combine references to show a reasonable likelihood of prevailing. Motivation may come from many sources (see guidance above) and need not be a precise teaching in the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources that can supply motivation to combine
rubrics_metrics.description: A need or problem known in the field at the time of invention and addressed by the patent can provide a reason for combining elements; other sources include market forces, design incentives, interrelated teachings of multiple patents, background knowledge, creativity, and common sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documented problems (e.g., safety concerns) and known solutions or recognized alternatives in the field can support motivation to combine. Use contemporaneous materials, admissions, publications, or other record evidence to show what artisans understood or sought to address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of success standard (not absolute)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show obviousness, the expectation of success need only be reasonable, not absolute. It is sufficient to show that a proposed combination would have been a suitable option for a person of ordinary skill (Intel Corp. v. PACT XPP).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioner need not prove the combination is the best or that it would achieve perfect/complete success—only that a reasonable expectation of success existed on the record at institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution-stage burden vs trial burden
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a significant difference between a petitioner's burden to establish a 'reasonable likelihood of success' at institution and actually proving invalidity by a preponderance of the evidence at trial (TriVascular).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess sufficiency of the petition for institution under the lower 'reasonable likelihood' standard; do not conflate institution with final invalidity proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of expert testimony: conclusory or anecdotal testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert declarations that merely offer conclusory assertions without underlying factual support are entitled to little weight. Expert testimony supported only by personal, anecdotal stories is likewise inadequate (Xerox; In re Ethicon; TQ Delta; Kyocera; Fed. R. Evid. 702 advisory notes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relying on expert evidence, ensure the expert explains how their experience leads to the conclusion, why the experience suffices, and how it reliably applies to the facts. Do not place weight on personal practices or anecdotes that do not show what a person of ordinary skill in the art would have known or done.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory consideration of secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: When evidence of secondary considerations has been made of record, 'the decision-maker is not free to ignore' it; the obviousness inquiry requires examination of all Graham factors (Updated Guidance; In re Huai-Hung Kao; Kinetic Concepts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address any secondary considerations presented (e.g., commercial success, long-felt but unsolved need, failure of others, copying, unexpected results, simultaneous invention) and explain their weight in the obviousness analysis rather than omitting them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous invention as objective evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Simultaneous (near-simultaneous) invention may bear on obviousness by (1) showing the level of skill in the art and (2) constituting objective evidence that persons of ordinary skill understood the problem and a solution to that problem (Regents v. Broad; Ecolochem; Geo. M. Martin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider independently made inventions and contemporaneous disclosures (including some post‑dating references) as persuasive evidence that the claimed invention was within ordinary skill; demonstrate timing (a comparatively short space of time) and independent development to bolster the inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of post-dating references to show level of skill
rubrics_metrics.description: References that postdate the claimed invention may be relied upon to show the level of ordinary skill in the art at or around the time the invention was made (MPEP §§ 2141.03, 2124).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, use later publications, publications or demonstrations (e.g., online videos) to illuminate what artisans understood or attempted, especially for simultaneous invention evidence—while recognizing such references are not prior art for anticipation/obviousness proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretionary denial under 35 U.S.C. § 314(a) and General Plastic/Valve framework
rubrics_metrics.description: PTAB may exercise discretion to deny institution under § 314(a) applying General Plastic factors and considering precedential Valve cases; one key consideration is whether a later petitioner has a 'significant relationship' to a prior petitioner (e.g., same party or substantially aligned interests/products).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether alleged serial or related petitions involve the same party or a significant relationship such that discretionary denial is warranted. Mere co-respondent status (e.g., joint participation in an ITC proceeding) or court-ordered coordination does not by itself establish the significant relationship contemplated by precedent. Distinct accused products and lack of interactions/agreement regarding the accused products weigh against discretionary denial.
